title: Looking back: year two
hookLine: the Buddha's words, read in order
tomorrow: which beginner sent the Buddha his two chief disciples?

lines: EACH TEACHER RUNS DOWN THE REST.
cards: Four tabs open, four reviews of the same thing, each one sure the others are wrong. A town in the suttas lived with that.
Wandering teachers kept passing through Kesaputta, each praising his own teaching and running down the rest. So the Kalamas, the people there, went to the Buddha and said it plainly: we're in doubt.
Which of these teachers is speaking the truth? He's one more teacher passing through. They're asking him to judge his rivals.
What he says next is not what a salesman would say.

teach.b: He says: it's fitting that you doubt.

Then he lists what not to lean on by itself: what you've heard over and over, tradition, rumor, a scripture, clever reasoning, a view you already like, a speaker who seems capable, even the thought, this monk is our teacher.

Instead, he says, when you know for yourselves that a thing is unwholesome, blamed by the wise, and leads to harm when taken up, let it go. When you know it leads to welfare and happiness, take it up.
And he doesn't leave them alone with that. He walks them through it.
Greed, hatred, delusion: when they arise in a person, is it for welfare or for harm? Harm, they say. And someone free of them?
Welfare. They worked it out themselves, with him asking the questions. Notice what he didn't say.
He didn't tell them to throw out every teacher, or to trust their gut alone. He pointed to what the wise blame and praise, and asked them to look. That's year two in one scene.
The Buddha's own words, read in order, keep handing the test back.
Buddhists have a word for the teaching that fits: ehipassiko, come and see.
Not take my word for it. Come and see. So reading the suttas isn't the opposite of testing them.

how: Buddhists read and chant the suttas at home and in temples; some teachers point to the Kalama Sutta when they invite students to test a teaching in their own practice.

o: giving up on the path once a hard stretch has begun
turning to a past year of the path to see what it gave
measuring yourself against how others have done

games.q: the Kalamas' question — tap the pairs.
p: each praised his own, ran down the rest

s: the Kalama Sutta says trust nothing but your own gut
it says know for yourselves what leads to harm or welfare, and it names what the wise blame. then he walks them through it.
the Buddha told the Kalamas their doubt was fitting
his first answer: it's fitting that you doubt.

games.q: your cousin swears by a morning routine from a video and wants you to try it because the guy has a huge following. what would the Kalama test ask first?
o: when you actually do it, what does it lead to: harm, or welfare?
how big the following is; that many people can't all be wrong.
nothing; the Buddha said never to try what anyone tells you.
games.why: not the crowd, and not 'trust nothing'. the Buddha told the Kalamas to watch what a thing does when taken up: harm, or welfare.

practice: Find a pen and anything to write on. Write one line of the Buddha's that you've actually tried in your own life, and under it, in a few words, what you saw happen.
Then rest your eyes on the page for the rest of the sit, the words and the test side by side.

wordCard.voice: Looking back, at year two: the discourses read in order, and the morning he told the Kalamas to see for themselves.

orig.note: Pali: come and see; said of the teaching, which invites you to look for yourself.

carryVoice: Your line: his own words. Read them, then let your life do the checking. Two days up the summit.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.65 (Kalama Sutta, also called Kesaputtiya Sutta)
Majjhima Nikaya 7 (the recollection of the Dhamma: 'come and see')
